Martin Casado:

"I really think the big disruption of AI is the fact that you can throw capital at problems. In the history of tech, you haven't been able to do that, because it was always an engineering problem, which just doesn't scale. 

The biggest shift with AI is I can take 20 people, give them a billion dollars, and they can use that. Do they make 500 million from that billion or two billion? I have no idea. But the fact that you can productively use that money is so new.

We've turned this into a capital resourcing problem, and we're capital allocators. We're in this very strategic position to help drive the future in a much more direct way than we ever have been before.

If you look at Anthropic and OpenAI, they've probably raised more money in aggregate than the entire downstream ecosystem combined. 

They are these mechanisms of turning money into growth."

$COHR earnings transcript TLDR:

Q: On $LITE + $MRVL merger.

A. Customers will prefer an independent optical supplier without competitive conflicts (opportunity for other merchant laser suppliers)

Q: Loop Capital asked about 2028 laser industry oversupply.

A: No oversupply risk by 2028. Coherent’s entire current internal InP production is consumed by its own products while its expanding capacity.

Q: On Chinese laser competition for CPO UHP lasers

A: “We really only have one competitor” (hinting at $LITE). 

Q: On financing concerns for capacity expansion during this market scare

A: Customer LTAs have prepayments, which are used for product capacity orders

2027 completely sold out, LTAs extend to 2030, customers placing orders into 2028.

Q: On laser technology for CPO scale up from Bernstein, whether it’s VCSELs or CW lasers.

A: CW for CPO scale out and scale up for 2026-2027.

2029-2030 sees scale in and chip to chip using micro-VCSELs, and 2028 opportunities for NPO scale up.

So technology of choice is CW for CPO.

- Coherent is seeing pricing power and raising margin targets, supporting view optical players get additional leverage for margin expansion

- Massive new $20B 5Y LTA, anchored by UHP CW lasers, with other optical products mixed in

- demand comes from growth in DC and conversion of copper interconnects to optics. The latter is bandwidth requirements, independent of DC growth.

slower compute growth can coexist with sharply rising optical content per system

TLDR:

- nothing quite showing optical demand like $20B in LTAs anchored by high power lasers from 1 customer alone (not your frontier labs type commitments)

- no industry wide laser oversupply risk by 2028 for InP lasers/EML 

- financing funded by revenue from LTAs and purchase orders.

- doesn’t see Chinese competition for high end lasers, commentary casts doubts over China capability + capacity expansion claims

- CW lasers weapon of choice for CPO, blended margins going up for optical players

- optics more isolated in the event of a DC slowdown 

Quite wild to see fundamentals of optical players improve so much, while overall valuations crash.

For companies like $SIVE / $AAOI, the demand imbalance for lasers are so severe

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

And obviously haircut growth valuations (but not to the point where demand collapses to 0).

Yet we're seeing everything in AI trade is getting lumped up together as something that requires heavy financing + not profitable.

There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

1. U.S. stocks had a powerful post-election rally on today, with the Dow Jones surging more than 3%, its strongest day since April 2025, as investors welcomed the removal of election uncertainty following Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress. The biggest catalyst was a sharp collapse in oil prices, driven by expectations that the new political landscape could increase pressure to resolve the Iran conflict, potentially easing energy costs, reducing inflationary pressures, and improving the outlook for consumers and businesses. Mega-cap technology stocks, including Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT, Apple $AAPL, and Alphabet $GOOGL, rallied as falling Treasury yields and improving risk appetite supported equities. However, the semiconductor and AI infrastructure sectors moved sharply in the opposite direction, with Micron $MU, Sandisk $SNDK, Marvell $MRVL, and CoreWeave $CRWV facing significant selling pressure. Investors are increasingly concerned that a Democratic Congress could introduce stricter data center regulations, permitting restrictions, and higher costs for AI infrastructure development, potentially slowing the pace of capital investment. 

2. President Donald Trump said he is not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, while defending his administration's military campaign against Iran following Republican losses in the midterm elections. Trump acknowledged that it was “largely true” that Republicans lost because of the Iran war, citing the impact of surging oil and gasoline prices on voters. However, when asked whether the conflict was worth the political and economic consequences, Trump responded “yes,” arguing that the United States had little choice because Iran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon. On the possibility of ending the conflict, Trump declared that “the Iran war will end whenever I want it to,” signaling that he believes the timing of any conclusion remains under his control.

Adjusted EBITDA jumped 31% to $2.96B, ahead of consensus, while free cash flow reached $2.54B, highlighting continued profitability and cash generation. Gross bookings climbed 20% to $59.82B, supported by 215M monthly active platform consumers, up 14% YoY, and 4.1B trips, up 16%. By segment, Delivery revenue surged 23% to $5.49B, Freight revenue increased 34% to $1.76B, while Mobility revenue declined 2% to $7.52B. Looking ahead, Uber guided Q4 adjusted EBITDA to $3.13B–$3.23B, with gross bookings of $63.25B–$65.25B and adjusted EPS of $0.95–$0.99. Management also highlighted accelerating progress in autonomous transportation, expecting approximately 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on Uber's platform by year-end and more than 2,000 in 2027, as the company increasingly focuses on commercializing robotaxi services at scale.

4. AMD $AMD has dramatically increased its unconditional purchase commitments to $48.8B, up 4x from $12.2B at the end of 2025 and $30.3B in June, according to its latest 10-Q filing, highlighting the enormous supply chain investments required to support its accelerating AI infrastructure business. Approximately $33.4B of these commitments are due by the end of 2027, primarily covering semiconductor wafers, advanced memory, substrates, and packaging capacity. AMD also disclosed $6.2B in cloud computing commitments, $13.3B in data center leases it expects to assign or sublease to partners, and up to $8.5B in guarantees covering partners' lease and debt obligations. Notably, lease guarantees nearly doubled to $7.7B from $4.1B in June, although AMD reported no partner defaults or guarantee payments to date. 

5. Alphabet $GOOGL plans to invest $15B in Malaysia during 2027 and 2028, significantly expanding its presence in Southeast Asia through new data center campuses, clean energy infrastructure, water security initiatives, and workforce training programs, according to Reuters. The investment highlights Google's accelerating commitment to AI and cloud computing infrastructure as demand for computing capacity continues to grow across the region. Beyond data center construction, the initiative will focus on securing reliable electricity, sustainable water resources, and skilled workers needed to support large-scale AI operations.

The proposed five-year agreement would have provided Tencent access to as many as 100,000 advanced AI chips housed in Oracle data centers across Southeast Asia, representing Tencent's largest overseas AI computing arrangement. The deal would have allowed Tencent to access advanced semiconductor technology that remains restricted within China, prompting U.S. officials to raise national security concerns with Oracle. Meanwhile, senior Chinese officials reportedly urged Tencent to prioritize domestic semiconductor suppliers, adding pressure from Beijing. Although overseas AI chip leasing remains permitted under existing regulations, the agreement was reportedly abandoned amid mounting geopolitical pressure from both governments. 

7. Coherent $COHR delivered a strong Q1 FY2027 earnings beat, with revenue surging 50% YoY to $2.37B, exceeding the $2.31B estimate, while adjusted EPS jumped 80% to $2.09, beating expectations of $1.97. Non-GAAP operating income reached $550M, ahead of the $527M estimate, while gross margins expanded 184 basis points to 40.6%, reflecting improving profitability. The standout was Data Center & Communications revenue, which surged 79% YoY to $1.95B, exceeding the $1.86B estimate, driven by accelerating demand for optical networking and AI infrastructure connectivity, while Industrial revenue declined 15% to $418.6M. Looking ahead, Coherent guided Q2 adjusted EPS to $2.28–$2.48, above the $2.21 consensus, with expected gross margins of 40%–42%. Management also expects FY2027 pro forma revenue growth to exceed 60% and anticipates achieving its first quarter with non-GAAP gross margins above 45% before the end of 2028, highlighting continued operating leverage as AI data center demand accelerates.

8. 9. Intel $INTC CEO Lip-Bu Tan purchased 150,000 shares of Intel stock on November 2 at an average price of approximately $64.73 per share, representing a personal investment of roughly $9.7M, according to an SEC filing. The sizable insider purchase represents a notable vote of confidence from Intel's chief executive as the company continues executing its turnaround strategy, expanding its AI and data center business, and investing in its next-generation foundry manufacturing capabilities. The transaction highlights Tan's willingness to increase his personal exposure to Intel's long-term performance as investors assess the sustainability of its recovery.

10. Big Tech stock buybacks are collapsing as AI infrastructure spending takes priority, with combined share repurchases by Alphabet $GOOGL, Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT, Meta $META, and Oracle $ORCL reportedly falling to just $4.4B in Q3 2026, their lowest quarterly level since Q3 2017. The slowdown comes as hyperscalers commit hundreds of billions of dollars toward AI data centers, GPUs, networking equipment, and power infrastructure, increasingly prioritizing capacity expansion over returning cash to shareholders. The trend signals a significant transformation in Big Tech's capital allocation strategy, with AI investments absorbing cash that might otherwise have supported stock repurchases, potentially reducing an important source of demand for their shares.

The transaction, described as the largest GPU financing arrangement on record, involves an Apollo-backed entity purchasing approximately $47.3B in NVIDIA $NVDA GPUs and related equipment, primarily next-generation Rubin chips, funded through roughly $40B in debt and a $7B lease prepayment from SpaceX. The debt package includes an $8.3B senior-secured loan alongside multiple bond tranches, with the financing structured so that the Apollo-backed entity owns the equipment while SpaceX leases the GPUs for approximately five years. The arrangement is designed to keep the financing debt off SpaceX's balance sheet, although the company remains obligated to make lease payments even if equipment is damaged or operations are disrupted.
